name: Chlorodehydromethyltestosterone (Turinabol / Oral Turinabol)
lead: Chlorodehydromethyltestosterone (CDMT, DHCMT), sold as Oral-Turinabol and nicknamed Tbol, is an oral anabolic-androgenic steroid, the 4-chloro derivative of metandienone. It was the first original product of the East German pharmaceutical company Jenapharm, patented in 1961, introduced clinically in 1965 and discontinued in 1994 [1].

In physique culture it is discussed as an oral anabolic that lifters stack with testosterone in pursuit of muscle size and strength, and therefore the fuller, more muscular frame they are aiming for [11][14]. These are claims from practitioners; no published trial has tested the drug for physique outcomes.

It is best known as the central drug in East Germany's state doping programme, which according to Wikipedia ran from about 1968 to 1989 and gave the steroid to roughly 10,000 athletes, often described to them as vitamins [1]. Long-lasting urinary metabolites identified in 2012 allowed retrospective re-testing of stored Olympic samples [1].

Published clinical research on Oral-Turinabol as a treatment is scarce. The literature consists largely of metabolism and detection studies, plus isolated case reports of harm [2][5]. It is a controlled substance in several countries and prohibited in sport [1].
infobox: US Schedule III; UK Class C; Brazil Class C5; WADA-prohibited [1]

paras: Wikipedia reports that chemist Albert Stachowiak proposed combining the structures of clostebol and metandienone, producing a compound that became Jenapharm's first original product [1]. After its clinical introduction in 1965, it became the main steroid in a secret state-run doping programme (State Plan Topic 14.25), with athletes often given tablets described to them as vitamins [1]. Researchers Franke and Berendonk documented the programme from East German archives in the 1990s [1]. Later, the IOC re-analysed stored samples from the 2008 and 2012 Games using a method for long-term CDMT metabolites and reported positives among weightlifters and sprinters [1].

The East German doping system began in the 1960s with a drive for Olympic prestige. According to Wikipedia's article on doping in East Germany, drugs became available to male athletes in 1966 and to women in 1968, doping became state policy in 1974, and Oral-Turinabol became the most common drug from the mid-1970s [12]. Estimates put the programme at perhaps 10,000 athletes, with up to 1,000 reported to have suffered serious lasting physical or psychological harm [12].

Reported effects included virilisation in female athletes, including adolescents, and the programme has been linked to miscarriages and cysts [12]. The secret police supervised the programme, and Stasi files opened in 1993 showed that many athletes had tested positive at an IOC-approved laboratory while official tests rarely caught them [12]. After reunification, two Dynamo Berlin doctors were convicted of administering hormones to underage girls between 1975 and 1984, and in 2016 the Bundestag created a 13.65 million euro fund for victims [12].

Human metabolism of Oral-Turinabol yields hydroxylated metabolites that are detectable in urine [2]. Studies have examined how human steroidogenic cytochrome P450 enzymes metabolise it [3] and have synthesised long-term metabolites for use as anti-doping reference material [4]. Wikipedia gives an elimination half-life of about 16 hours, but this figure is tagged as needing a citation [1].

Chemically, the compound was conceived by combining the structures of clostebol (4-chlorotestosterone) and metandienone [1]. Wikipedia lists oral bioavailability as high, with hepatic metabolism and urinary elimination [1]. Researchers have also shown that the brain enzyme CYP46A1 can metabolise it, and that it competes with cholesterol at that enzyme in vitro, which the authors suggest could be relevant to possible pathogenic effects [7]. Mass-spectrometry methods have been developed to screen urine for it alongside other 17-alkylated steroids [8], and spectroscopy work has targeted its illegal addition to food and drug products [9].

Controlled trials of its adverse effects have not been published. A 17-alkylated structure is the feature associated with liver effects among oral steroids: a T Nation poster notes that long-term use of related 17-alkylated steroids such as fluoxymesterone and methyltestosterone has been linked to hepatic pathology, listing chlorodehydromethyltestosterone among them [13]. A case report described an intratesticular leiomyosarcoma in a 32-year-old man after high-dose doping with the drug, with the authors raising a possible but unproven association [5]. Animal studies of anabolic steroids more broadly report impaired growth of the cardiac capillary bed in exercise-trained animals [6].

No studies found of Oral-Turinabol for appearance or physique. Human-related literature consists of metabolite identification [2][3][4] and a case report of an intratesticular leiomyosarcoma in a 32-year-old man after high-dose doping with the drug, in which the authors raised a possible but unproven association [5]. Animal work on anabolic steroids more broadly has reported effects on the heart, such as impaired growth of the cardiac capillary bed in exercise-trained animals [6].

The drug remains prohibited in sport. Wikipedia lists high-profile doping cases involving turinabol, including mixed martial artist Jon Jones after UFC 214 in 2017 and baseball player Colton Welker in 2021 [1]. In bodybuilding circles it is described under the nickname Tbol as an oral steroid associated with its East German history, though no published trials test those claims. Wikipedia reports that in May 2021 Colton Welker received an 80-game suspension after testing positive [1].

In forum culture the drug is usually called Tbol or Turanabol. Veteran-written primers on T Nation described it as an oral steroid developed in the early 1960s, and members describe it in the context of stacks with injectable testosterone [10][14]. Other posters say counterfeit or mislabelled oral products are common on the gray market, with one claiming that most oral steroids sold under names such as turinabol are actually stanozolol or something else [15].

timeline.event: Drugs become available to East German male (1966) and female (1968) athletes [12].
Doping becomes state policy in East Germany [12].
East German state doping programme ends with the state's collapse [1].
Long-term metabolites reported, enabling retrospective detection [1].
Jon Jones tests positive for turinabol after UFC 214 [1].

lore.intro: On T Nation the compound appears in stack discussions, history threads and gray-market warnings [10][11][14][15].

claims.claim: Tbol is a suitable oral for people who aromatize heavily
claims.believers: One poster asks whether turinabol would be a better option because of heavy aromatization, and others mention pairing it with testosterone for strength and muscle [11][16].
claims.experts: No published trial has compared its anabolic effects or side effects with other steroids; Wikipedia gives no androgenic-to-anabolic ratio [1].

claims.claim: The East German programme shows the drug builds muscle and athletic performance
claims.believers: Forum posts point to its role in East Germany's medal tally as proof of efficacy [10].
claims.experts: Archival work by Franke and Berendonk documented the programme [1], and later accounts record serious harms including virilisation of female athletes and legal convictions [12].

claims.claim: Oral steroids sold under the Turinabol name are often something else
claims.believers: A T Nation member states that oral products from some markets are diluted or mislabelled stanozolol or dianabol [15].
claims.experts: Analytical chemists have developed detection methods for illegal anabolic steroid additives in food and drug products [9].

claims.claim: Like other 17-alkylated orals, it stresses the liver
claims.believers: Posters cite studies showing liver-enzyme elevations with related steroids [13].
claims.experts: No published trial has measured liver outcomes for this drug; the structural class is associated with hepatic effects [13].

card.summary: The oral steroid of East German doping fame; well documented in history and detection science, untested as a treatment.
card.note: Banned in sport; controlled in the US, UK and Brazil.

quick.overview:
Oral-Turinabol was Jenapharm's oral steroid, made from metandienone with an added chlorine atom. It was used for decades in East Germany's state doping programme.

Its reputation among lifters comes from that history. No clinical trials test it for muscle or appearance.
quick.mechanism: It is an androgen-receptor agonist derived from metandienone. Its 17-methyl group allows oral use, and it is metabolised in the liver to metabolites that can be detected in urine for a long time.
quick.risks: Documented evidence is limited to case reports and general anabolic-steroid concerns, including a case report of a testicular tumour after high-dose use. It is banned in sport and controlled in several countries.

chain: Oral 17-alkylated anabolic-androgenic steroid acts at androgen receptors
Users report added lean mass and strength
angle.text: Bodybuilders and strength athletes who use it say it supports muscle gain and strength, and some say it suits people who report heavy aromatization of other compounds. This is the community's account; the drug has no modern clinical programme and is controlled or banned in most settings.
